190.title: Seven baskets (Mark 8:1–10)
190.hook: a second feeding, in Gentile country, four thousand fed
190.howItsDone: Many churches call communion the Eucharist, from the Greek word for giving thanks, and many Christians volunteer at food banks and shared meals that feed people beyond their own congregation.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ephphatha, be opened, sighed toward heaven. Your line was a sound you usually ignore.

Ever had déjà vu so strong you almost laughed? A huge crowd, out in the middle of nowhere. Nothing to eat. Jesus turns to the disciples and says, I feel for these people. And the disciples, who watched five thousand fed from five loaves just two chapters ago, ask where anyone could find bread out here. You want to shake them. Then again, how often does anyone forget what already happened to them?
screen: `A HUGE CROWD, AGAIN.` → `NOTHING TO EAT, AGAIN.` → `WHERE COULD WE FIND BREAD?`

segments.voice: This time Jesus speaks first, in the old King James Bible: "I have compassion on the multitude, because they have now been with me three days, and have nothing to eat." They've stayed so long their food ran out. Some, he says, came from far away; send them home hungry and they'll collapse on the road. The disciples answer: "From whence can a man satisfy these men with bread here in the wilderness?" He asks the same question as before: what have you got? Seven loaves, and a few small fish. He has everyone sit on the ground, gives thanks, breaks, and hands it to the disciples to give out. The Greek for gave thanks is the word that gives us eucharist, the name many churches use for communion. Four thousand eat and are satisfied, and seven baskets are left over. Why tell a second feeding at all? Look at the map. Yesterday Jesus was in the ten cities, Gentile country. Many readers think this crowd is mostly Gentile, the same people the Syrophoenician mother spoke for. The first time, twelve baskets, like the twelve tribes of Israel. This time, seven, a number of fullness and completeness, and some hear the nations in it. The crumbs she asked for became a meal with leftovers. Even the baskets are different. The first feeding used a Greek word for a small wicker basket; this one uses a word for a big one, large enough, in Acts, to lower Paul over a city wall. Then they sail off to a place called Dalmanutha. Nobody today knows where that was.
screen: `THREE DAYS, AND NOTHING TO EAT.` · `HE GAVE THANKS — EUCHARIST.` · `TWELVE BASKETS, THEN SEVEN.` · `DALMANUTHA: NOBODY KNOWS WHERE.`

segments.voice: Picture the people you feed without thinking, family, friends, the office birthday, then look just past the edge of that circle: a neighbor you don't know, a coworker from another team, a stranger at a shelter or a food bank who's been waiting a while and came from far. Choose one way you could feed someone outside your circle. If you pray, you can give thanks for what you have, the way he did before he broke the bread.
Seven baskets. The leftovers from a second feeding, four thousand, in Gentile country, enough again.
Your line: enough again. Four thousand fed, and seven baskets to spare. That's day one hundred ninety.

191.title: Hard hearts in a boat (Mark 8:11–21)
191.hook: they've forgotten bread and worry, after two feedings
191.howItsDone: Some Christians keep a habit of remembering God's help in the past, through gratitude journals, testimonies or prayers of thanksgiving, as a way of meeting present worries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seven baskets: four thousand fed in Gentile country. Your line was enough again.

One loaf. That's the whole inventory. A few verses back, seven baskets of leftovers. Now the disciples are crossing the lake again, somebody checks the bag, and Mark says they had forgotten to take bread: one loaf with them, and that's all. It's the wallet-left-on-the-counter moment, out on the water. While they mutter about lunch, Jesus is trying to tell them something else entirely. They miss it, and Mark doesn't tidy the scene up for them.
screen: `ONE LOAF IN THE BOAT.` → `THE BREAD THEY FORGOT.` → `THEY MISS WHAT HE SAYS.`

segments.voice: Just before they sailed, some Pharisees had asked Jesus for a sign from heaven, proof on demand. He sighed deeply and refused: no sign will be given to this generation. Now in the boat he warns, in the old King James Bible: "Take heed, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, and of the leaven of Herod." Leaven, you might remember from day twenty-four, is the bit of old dough that works invisibly through a whole batch. Mark doesn't define it here. Some readers take it as an attitude that spreads: demanding proof, playing power games. And the disciples say to each other, he's talking about bread because we forgot to bring any. So the questions come fast: "perceive ye not yet, neither understand? have ye your heart yet hardened? Having eyes, see ye not? and having ears, hear ye not? and do ye not remember?" Then a quiz. When I broke five loaves for five thousand, how many baskets of leftovers? Twelve, they say. And the seven for four thousand? Seven. And he says, "How is it that ye do not understand?" No answer. They've watched thousands fed, twice, and they're worried about lunch with him sitting right there. And notice the one loaf in the boat. Some readers hear a quiet hint: they're not as short of bread as they think, because the one who fed the crowds is on board. Mark leaves them there, mid-crossing, with two counts of baskets and one loaf in the bag.

segments.voice: Go back to a time you were sure you wouldn't make it, when money, time, strength or hope was short, and somehow there was enough: someone showed up, a door opened, you got through. Count the baskets, so to speak: what was left over afterward? Hold that memory next to whatever you're worried about today, and if you pray, you can give thanks for that time.

192.title: Men like trees (Mark 8:22–26)
192.hook: the only two-stage healing: first blurry, then clear
192.howItsDone: Some Christians describe faith as a journey rather than a single moment, and some churches pray for healing more than once, taking comfort from the second touch in this story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one loaf in a boat, two feedings forgotten, and a warning about leaven. Your line was do you not yet understand?

If you've ever worn glasses, you know the moment at the eye doctor. They click through the lenses. Better like this? Or like this? The chart goes from smudge, to almost, to sharp. Today's healing happens a lot like that. At Bethsaida, people bring a blind man to Jesus, and Mark tells it in two stages, with a pause in the middle. He even tells us what the man saw halfway through.

Jesus takes the man by the hand and leads him out of the village. Picture that walk: a blind man holding a stranger's hand down a dirt road. Then Jesus spits on his eyes, lays his hands on him, and asks, do you see anything? In the old King James Bible, the man looks up and says, "I see men as trees, walking." Blurry shapes, tall and moving. He can tell they're people only because trees don't walk. It's an honest answer; he doesn't pretend. So Jesus lays his hands on his eyes a second time, "and he was restored, and saw every man clearly." Clearly, and far: lexicons give Mark's Greek word as plainly, even at a distance. Why would Mark tell a healing in two stages? He doesn't say. But look where he puts it. Just before, Jesus asked the disciples, having eyes, see ye not? Tomorrow, Peter will say who Jesus is, and then, in the very next breath, prove he only half understands it. Some readers think this blind man is a picture of the disciples. They see something. It's blurry. People look like trees. They'll need a second touch. Read that way, the story makes room for an honest halfway: the right answer to do you see? can be, sort of. And in Mark, sort of isn't where it ends. There's a second touch.
screen: `LED BY THE HAND OUT OF TOWN.` · `I SEE MEN AS TREES, WALKING.` · `A SECOND TOUCH, THEN CLEARLY.` · `A PICTURE OF THE DISCIPLES.`

Ask it honestly, the way Jesus asked the man, do you see anything yet? and if the answer is sort of, blurry, men like trees, let that be all right. If you pray, you can ask for the second touch; if not, just thank yourself for getting halfway.

193.title: You are the Christ (Mark 8:27–30)
193.hook: at Caesarea Philippi, Peter says it: you are the Messiah, the anointed one
193.carry: who do you say I am?
193.howItsDone: Christians confess Jesus as the Christ, and in churches that use the Creeds, the congregation says it aloud in worship; some Christians use Peter's question as a regular prompt for personal prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a blind man at Bethsaida saw men like trees, walking, and then every man clearly. Your line was sight comes in stages.

Someone new starts at work, and before anyone really knows them, the theories begin. He's the one who used to be at that other place. She's like the last manager, only quieter. Now, on a road far in the north, near the towns of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks his friends a simple question: "Whom do men say that I am?" They have the talk ready. Some say John the Baptist. Some say Elijah. Some say one of the prophets. Then he turns the question around, and there's nowhere to hide: "But whom say ye that I am?" And Peter answers.
screen: `A ROAD FAR IN THE NORTH.` → `WHOM DO MEN SAY THAT I AM?` → `BUT WHOM SAY YE?`

segments.voice: Peter says four words in the old King James Bible: "Thou art the Christ." Christ is not Jesus's last name. There was no Mr. and Mrs. Christ. It's a title. The Greek word is Christos, and it means the anointed one. It translates a Hebrew word, mashiach, which comes into English as Messiah. Anointed means oil poured on your head. In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet Samuel pours oil on young David to mark him as king, and priests were anointed too. In Jesus's day there were Jews who hoped for an anointed one, a king from David's family. When Peter says Christ, he's saying: you are that one. Back in the storm on the lake, the disciples asked, what manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? Now someone finally says it out loud. Mark's very first line had already told the reader: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." The disciples just took half the book to catch up. Then the strange part: Jesus charges them to tell no one. Scholars still argue about why, and Mark never fully explains. One hint comes in the very next scene: the word Christ meant something different to Peter than it would turn out to mean. Christians confess it in their creeds: Jesus is the Christ. But notice how he asked. Not what do people say. What do you say.
screen: `WHOM SAY YE THAT I AM?` · `CHRIST IS A TITLE, NOT A SURNAME.` · `ANOINTED: OIL ON A KING'S HEAD.` · `HIS ORDER: TELL NO ONE.` · then, large: `THOU ART THE CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Maybe you pray to Jesus every day, maybe you're learning about him for someone you love, maybe you honestly don't know; imagine the road, and the question turned toward you: who do you say I am? Don't reach for the right answer, or the answer your family gives; find your own word, even if it's teacher, or stranger, or I'm not sure yet. If you pray, you can simply say what you find, and just be honest.
Christ. From the Greek Christos, the anointed one, the same word as the Hebrew Messiah. A title, not a surname.

194.title: Take up your cross (Mark 8:31–38)
194.hook: Peter rebukes him about suffering, is called Satan, and hears: lose your life to save it
194.howItsDone: Some Christians speak of their own small sacrifices as carrying the cross, and some take on a daily act of self-giving; in Lent especially, churches that keep the season invite people to give something up for the sake of others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, near Caesarea Philippi, Peter called him the Christ. Your line was who do you say I am?

Thou art the Christ. Top of the class. Then, straight away, Jesus starts to explain what that will mean, and none of it is what they hoped to hear. He'll suffer many things. He'll be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes. He'll be killed. And after three days he'll rise again. He says it openly, Mark adds. So Peter, like any loyal friend, takes Jesus aside, quietly, and tells him off. No. Not that. Not you. And Jesus turns around, looks at the others, and answers Peter in front of all of them.
screen: `TOP OF THE CLASS.` → `HE MUST SUFFER.` → `PETER TAKES HIM ASIDE.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible: "Get thee behind me, Satan." From top of the class to Satan in a handful of verses. It sounds brutal. But in Hebrew, satan means an adversary, the one who stands in your way. One way to hear it: Peter has put himself in front of Jesus, blocking the road. Get behind me: go back to following. Then he calls the crowd over, with his disciples: "Whosoever will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me." Today a cross can be a necklace or a steeple. To that crowd it was a Roman way of putting people to death, in public, and as Mark will later show, a cross was carried through the streets to the place of death. The words may well have made them flinch. Then the riddle at the center: "For whosoever will save his life shall lose it; but whosoever shall lose his life for my sake and the gospel's, the same shall save it." Grip your life too tight and it slips away. Christians have read this in more than one way. For the early church, under persecution, it could mean dying for the faith. Luke's version adds the word daily, and some hear it as ordinary self-giving: the parent up at 3am, the friend who shows up. And some churches today say plainly what it does not mean: it is not a command to stay in harm or abuse. The verse itself holds both halves, side by side: lose, and save.

195.title: Listen to him (Mark 9:1–13)
195.hook: the transfiguration, and the one instruction from the cloud: listen to him
195.carry: let it change what you do
195.howItsDone: Many churches celebrate the Transfiguration as a feast, on August 6 in the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican calendars, and many Protestant churches read the story on the Sunday before Lent; Christians often speak of listening to Jesus through reading the Gospels and in silent prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter heard take up your cross. Your line was lose it to find it.

Six days later, Mark says, Jesus takes three friends, Peter, James and John, up a high mountain, just the four of them. Up there, he changes in front of them. His clothes turn shining, dazzling white, and Mark, who loves a homely detail, says they were whiter than any laundryman on earth could get them. Then two figures appear, talking with him: Elijah and Moses, great prophets from centuries before. And Peter, bless him, has to say something. It's good for us to be here! Let's build three shelters: one for you, one for Moses, one for Elijah. Mark adds, gently: "For he wist not what to say; for they were sore afraid." He didn't know what to say, so he said something. Everyone has been Peter.
screen: `A HIGH MOUNTAIN, JUST FOUR.` → `WHITER THAN ANY LAUNDRY.` → `LET'S BUILD THREE SHELTERS.`

segments.voice: While Peter is still planning construction, a cloud comes down and covers them, and a voice speaks out of it. In the King James Bible: "This is my beloved Son: hear him." One sentence of introduction, one instruction. Not build. Not explain. Hear him. The Greek word means listen, and in the Bible listening is never just sound in the ears. In Hebrew, the same word covers hearing and obeying. To really listen is to let it change what you do. Notice what the voice doesn't say: listen to Moses and Elijah too. Many Christians read those two as standing for the Law and the Prophets, the whole Hebrew Bible, gathered around Jesus. Then, suddenly, they look around and see no one any more, only Jesus, with them. The cloud and the glow are gone: an ordinary man on a mountain, and the instruction to listen. Mark never names the mountain. Christian tradition since early centuries has pointed to Mount Tabor in Galilee, and others suggest Mount Hermon, much nearer Caesarea Philippi. On the way down he tells them to tell no one until he has risen from the dead, and they puzzle over what that could mean. Christians call this the transfiguration, from the Latin for being changed in form. Orthodox Christians hold it especially dear, and Catholic, Anglican and many other churches keep it as a feast on the sixth of August.
screen: `A CLOUD, AND ONE SENTENCE.` · `LISTEN MEANS HEAR AND DO.` · `NO ONE LEFT BUT JESUS.` · `A MOUNTAIN MARK NEVER NAMES.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY BELOVED SON: HEAR HIM.`

segments.voice: Don't plan anything, don't fix anything, don't build any shelters: just listen, first to the sounds of the room, then to the sounds far away, then to the quiet underneath. If a thought wants to talk, let it pass like a cloud. If you pray, you can hold the line hear him, and wait, without filling the silence.
Transfiguration, from Latin for being changed in form: the mountain where Jesus shone before Peter, James and John, and a voice said, listen.
Your line: let it change what you do. The voice gave one instruction: hear him. Day one hundred ninety-five, complete.

196.title: Help my unbelief (Mark 9:14–29)
196.hook: a desperate father: I believe; help my unbelief
196.howItsDone: Some Christians pray the father's words, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief," as a short prayer in times of doubt, and some pastors point to this story to say that faith and doubt can live together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on the mountain, a voice from the cloud gave one instruction: hear him. Your line was let it change what you do.

From the shining mountain straight down into a mess: a crowd, and an argument. The disciples who stayed behind have tried to heal a boy, and they couldn't. The boy's father pushes through. His son, he says, has a spirit that takes his speech, throws him to the ground, makes him foam and grind his teeth and go rigid. Since he was a child. It has thrown him into fire and into water. Years of nights like that, and now even the disciples have failed. His hope is worn thin. In the King James Bible he says: "if thou canst do any thing, have compassion on us, and help us." If.
screen: `DOWN FROM THE MOUNTAIN.` → `THE DISCIPLES COULDN'T.` → `IF THOU CANST DO ANY THING.`

segments.voice: Jesus catches the word and hands the if back. In the King James text: "If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth." And the father cries out, with tears: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both at once. I believe, and I don't. I trust you, and I'm terrified. He doesn't pretend. And Jesus doesn't send him away to come back when his faith is tidier. He heals the boy, and lifts him by the hand. In Mark's telling, half a faith, handed over honestly, is where it starts. The Greek word for unbelief is apistia, faith with a no in front of it. Some Christians call this verse a lifeline, because it puts doubt and faith in the same sentence. Readers today often notice that the boy's signs sound like epilepsy. Mark describes a spirit, and Christians understand stories like this in different ways. Later, the disciples ask privately why they failed. His answer, in the King James: "This kind can come forth by nothing, but by prayer and fasting." Now look back at the week. Seven baskets: enough again. Hard hearts in a boat: do you not yet understand? A blind man seeing men like trees. Peter: you are the Christ. Take up your cross. Listen to him. And now this father. Again and again this week, someone sees in part, and is helped further along.
screen: `IF THOU CANST?` · `I BELIEVE; HELP MY UNBELIEF.` · `BY PRAYER AND FASTING.` · `A WEEK OF SEEING IN PART.` · then, large: `LORD, I BELIEVE; HELP THOU MINE UNBELIEF.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you trust and one thing you doubt, about God, about yourself, about someone you love, and let them sit side by side without solving either. If you pray, you can say the father's words, slowly, as many times as you like: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. If you don't pray, you can simply say: some of me trusts, some of me doesn't, and that's where I am.
Apistia, faith with a no in front of it: a father's cry holding belief and doubt in the same breath, and it was enough.
Your line: bring the half you have. Half sure is enough to bring. Another week, done.
